name: Takayama ramen (Hida chuka soba)
ja: 高山ラーメン（飛騨中華そば）
text: The light shoyu chuka soba of Takayama in Hida. Explanatory sites describe it as a clear soy-flavoured soup paired with very thin, curly, low-hydration noodles that keep a firm bite. Some sources date its origin to about 1938 (Showa 13); another says the method of simmering the shoyu tare in the stockpot spread in postwar Takayama. Accounts differ in detail and are mostly secondary.
flavor: Clean, soy-forward and light, with thin curled noodles that stay springy.
use: Served as a plain bowl of chuka soba; judged on the balance of tare and soup and on noodle bite rather than richness.
craft: One source says tare and soup are cooked together rather than combined at the bowl, which fuses the seasoning into the stock. Pair it with a low-hydration, very fine noodle; thin low-hydration noodle is what gives the stated firmness. Origin dates vary by source, so do not state one date as settled.
src: Shin-Yokohama Ramen Museum Rapedia: Takayama ramen

name: Nagoya Taiwan ramen
text: A very spicy ramen from Nagoya, said to have originated at Misen (味仙), Imaike main shop, Chikusa-ku. Topping is Taiwan mince: ground pork stir-fried with garlic chives, bean sprouts and spring onion with chili and garlic, served over chicken-bone shoyu soup and Chinese noodles. The founder was from Taiwan and adapted Taiwanese danzai noodles; one source places the start in the 1970s. Despite the name it is a Nagoya invention.
flavor: Hot with chili and garlic, savoury minced pork, chive and sprout freshness over a shoyu-chicken soup.
use: Eaten as a single bowl; the mince is the seasoning, so it is stirred through the soup.
craft: The distinguishing technique is the stir-fried chili-garlic mince made with chive and sprouts, not the soup, which is a chicken-bone shoyu base. Dating and founder story come from commentary sites; confirm with the shop before quoting a year.
src: Nagoya Global Support: Taiwan ramen origin
BTJ Foodie Lab: Taiwan ramen history

name: Taiwan mazesoba (Nagoya)
text: A brothless, hot-mixed noodle bowl developed at Menya Hanabi (麺屋はなび), Takahata main shop in Nagoya, founded in 2008 by Shinyama Naoto. It took the already popular Taiwan ramen and served it without soup; word of mouth spread it. Sources describe it as a soup-less version of the Taiwan ramen concept.
flavor: Intense, spicy, garlicky and savoury, stirred into a thick coating.
use: Noodles and toppings are thoroughly mixed in the bowl before eating.
craft: The concept is Taiwan ramen's seasoned mince moved onto dry noodles, so seasoning must be strong enough to coat the noodles without soup to dilute it. Dates and attribution come from secondary sources; confirm with the shop.
src: Hanako: Nagoya Taiwan ramen and mazesoba

name: Tsukemen origin: Taishoken morisoba
ja: つけ麺（大勝軒・もりそば）
text: The most cited account credits Yamagishi Kazuo with developing and selling tsukemen as morisoba at Taishoken, Nakano, in 1955; he opened his own Taishoken in Higashi-Ikebukuro in 1961 serving tokusei morisoba. It began as a staff meal of leftover noodles dipped in soup and soy. For sale he used vinegar and sugar, inspired by hiyashi chuka, and made the noodle portion 30 percent larger than ramen. Another theory credits the founder of Marucho. Sources disagree on shop and year.
flavor: Sweet-sour, soy-based dipping soup with plump cold noodles.
use: Noodles are dipped in the soup; the large noodle portion defines the style.
craft: The original sauce balance is sweet and sour (vinegar and sugar) rather than rich, which is why the noodle portion is large. Dating (1955 Nakano vs 1961 Higashi-Ikebukuro) differs by source, so state the claim as attributed.
src: Japan Ramen Franchise Assoc.: History column 5

name: Musashino abura soba (Chinchintei)
text: Brothless noodles dressed with oil and a soy tare, associated with Musashino in western Tokyo. The origin is attributed to Chinchintei in Musashisakai and to Sanko in Kunitachi; Chinchintei's founding year is given as 1954 in some sources and 1957 in others. It is said to derive from a Chinese mixed noodle with the soup reduced, and from ramen-shop staff meals of the 1950s to 1960s. Chinchintei's tare is described as lard and soy sauce.
flavor: Sweet-soy richness carried by lard, brightened at the table by vinegar and chili oil.
use: Mixed in the bowl, then adjusted with table vinegar and rayu.
craft: Because there is no soup, the tare and fat carry everything; vinegar cuts the oil and rayu adds aroma and heat. Two competing origin shops and two founding dates exist, so attribute rather than assert.

name: Abura soba vs mazesoba
ja: 油そばとまぜそばの違い
text: The two are not strictly defined. Abura soba usually means the older simple style of soy tare and oil, while mazesoba is the broader or newer name covering richer varieties with more toppings and flavours, such as Nagoya's Taiwan mazesoba. One explanation holds that abura soba came first and the name mazesoba spread later.
flavor: Abura soba is plain and oily-soy; mazesoba is typically bolder and more layered.
use: Use abura soba for the classic tare, oil and table-vinegar format; use mazesoba where toppings and seasoning are the point.
craft: Treat the terms as menu conventions, not standards: decide by tare design and topping scheme rather than by name.

name: Hiroshima tsukemen
text: A cold-noodle, hot-chili dipping style associated with Hiroshima, traced to Shinkaen (新華園), opened in 1954 near the Irifune-cho tram stop; its menu name there is said to have been reimen. Noodles are medium-thick, straight and rinsed in cold water, served on a plate topped with chashu, boiled vegetables such as cabbage, and egg. The soy-based sauce carries chili, rayu, vinegar and plenty of sesame.
flavor: Sharp, hot and sour with sesame depth, against cold firm noodles.
use: Noodles are dipped in the spicy sauce; the cold noodles and vegetable toppings distinguish it from Kanto tsukemen.
craft: Cold-water rinsing of the noodles is part of the style. The sauce is built on chili, rayu, vinegar and sesame, so heat is adjusted by shop. The origin claim rests on Wikipedia-level sources.

name: Hiroshima shirunashi tantanmen
text: Brothless tantanmen presented by Hiroshima Prefecture as a spicy local noodle, and stated to have originated in Hiroshima. The prefecture's page describes mixing the spicy tare pooled at the bottom of the bowl with the sansho sprinkled on the noodles. It is served alongside spicy tsukemen as the two popular hot noodle dishes of Hiroshima city.
flavor: Hot with chili and numbing sansho, concentrated tare coating the noodles.
use: Mix the sauce from the bowl base with the noodles and sansho before eating.
craft: Mixing thoroughly is required because tare and sansho sit separately. The sources seen did not explain how it differs from Sichuan dan dan noodles or credit any individual chef, so avoid such claims.
src: Hiroshima Prefecture: Spicy noodles of Hiroshima
Kotrip: Hiroshima tsukemen and shirunashi tantan

name: Okayama ramen
text: Said to have begun in yatai and barracks in central Okayama City just after World War II. Soup is mainly chicken-bone shoyu or pork-bone shoyu, sometimes with a seafood accent, and noodles are mostly thin to medium-thin straight; curly noodles are rare. Okayama City is also noted for tonkatsu ramen. Sources disagree on whether pork-bone or chicken-bone shoyu is the standard.
flavor: Lightly sweet shoyu soup with clean thin noodles.
use: Served as shoyu ramen; local variants such as tonkatsu ramen appear in the city.
craft: Straight thin to medium-thin noodles are the usual match. Because sources conflict on the base soup, describe both chicken and pork-bone shoyu rather than one canon.

name: Kasaoka ramen
text: A local ramen of Kasaoka, Okayama. According to Wikipedia, it is defined by a chicken-bone shoyu soup and a topping of simmered kashiwa (old hen) meat, called nitori.
flavor: Chicken-led shoyu soup with firm, savoury simmered hen meat.
use: Served as a shoyu ramen topped with simmered hen meat.
craft: The distinguishing element is the simmered old-hen meat as topping; the sources seen give no further process details.

name: Kurume ramen
text: Kurume is widely credited as the birthplace of tonkotsu ramen: several sources say Miyamoto Tokio finished the prototype at the stall Nankin Senryo in 1937. He is said to have trained in Yokohama's Chinatown, and the early soup was not cloudy. Another account places the origin of the milky white soup at the stall Sanku in 1947.
flavor: Rich, milky pork-bone soup with a heavy pork aroma.
use: Served as tonkotsu ramen; the style is the reference point for Hakata and Nagahama styles.
craft: Two founding stories coexist: a 1937 prototype and a 1947 cloudy soup. Cite them as separate claims.
src: Shin-Yokohama Ramen Museum Rapedia: Kurume ramen

name: Nagahama ramen and kaedama
ja: 長浜ラーメンと替え玉
text: Nagahama in Chuo-ku, Fukuoka, is widely given as the birthplace of kaedama, the extra noodle portion. Very thin noodles were devised for workers at the fish market and, being quick to cook and prone to soften, were refilled in small portions. Ganso Nagahamaya is frequently named as the origin shop, with 1952 as its founding; other sources date it simply to the 1950s.
flavor: Pork-bone soup with very thin noodles that finish quickly.
use: Order the noodles in small portions and refill with kaedama to keep them firm.
craft: Ultra-thin noodles soften fast, so the kaedama system exists to serve noodles at the right firmness. Founding date and exact origin vary by source.
src: Jimo Hack Fukuoka: Origin of kaedama

name: Sasebo ramen
text: Sasebo shops commonly serve a light blend of chicken-bone and pork-bone soup with somewhat thick, soft noodles, topped with bean sprouts, wood ear, spring onion and chashu. Yatai-origin tonkotsu is the representative style; Oei-san is cited as a long-established shop founded in Showa 30 (1955) that started from a stall near the station. Many shops keep oden on the menu all year.
flavor: Mild, homely chicken and pork soup; some shops are oilier with angular noodles.
use: Often eaten with oden at the same shop.
craft: Noodle shape varies: some cut angular, slightly fine noodles linked to the Oei-san style. Treat descriptions as shop-dependent.

name: Sasebo kai-paitan (shellfish white broth)
ja: 佐世保貝白湯ラーメン
text: A recent Sasebo trend using shellfish stock instead of pork bone. One cited shop, Ramen Toride, builds paitan from clam, oyster, scallop and razor-clam-type matega from the Harioi area, plus vegetables, without pork bone.
flavor: Milky, marine and sweet-savoury shellfish stock.
use: Served as an emulsified white-broth ramen.
craft: The stock is made from several shellfish and vegetables rather than bone, so seasoning relies on shellfish extract. Described by a single shop in the sources seen.

name: Miyako soba
text: The soba of Miyako Island in Okinawa. Descriptions say its noodles are thin or flat, straight rather than crimped, in a light soup, with toppings placed under the noodles so they are hidden when served.
flavor: Light soup with straight, thin noodles.
use: Served with the toppings tucked beneath the noodles.
craft: The hidden-topping presentation is the local signature. Sources seen give no ratios or processing details.
src: Churasun: Okinawa soba, Miyako and Yaeyama

name: Yaeyama soba
text: The soba of the Yaeyama Islands (Ishigaki and others). Noodles are round in cross-section and without crimps; sources disagree on thickness, some saying thin and others slightly thicker than Okinawa mainland soki soba. The soup is described as sweeter than mainland soba, the pork is cut into strips, and pipaachi (Piper retrofractum) is a hallmark.
flavor: Sweeter soup, peppery floral heat from pipaachi.
use: Served with thin-cut pork and pipaachi added to taste.
craft: Round, uncrimped noodles and shredded pork distinguish it from mainland soki soba; verify noodle thickness locally because sources conflict.
src: Mikawa Shokudo: Soki soba vs Yaeyama soba

name: Soki soba
text: A form of Okinawa soba topped with soki, simmered pork spare ribs. Using bone-in ribs lets their flavour pass into the soup. It is a variety of Okinawa soba, whose standard bowl has sanmai-niku (simmered pork belly), kamaboko, pickled red ginger and spring onion.
flavor: Pork-rich soup with tender ribs.
use: Eaten as Okinawa soba with simmered ribs.
craft: Bone-in ribs release flavour into the soup. Cartilage soba is not covered in the sources seen.
src: Mikawa Shokudo: Soki soba vs Yaeyama soba

name: Mokubai soba (wood-ash noodles)
text: Okinawa soba noodles are normally made from wheat flour with kansui, salt and water, sometimes with oil finishing. Before the war the supernatant of wood-ash water was used in place of kansui, and some shops still serve noodles made this way as ash soba.
flavor: Alkaline-wheat character from ash lye.
use: Served as Okinawa soba at specialist shops.
craft: Wood-ash supernatant plays the role of the alkaline agent. Sources seen give no concentration or resting times.

name: Kiriba bante (cutter blade number)
text: The number that sets noodle thickness, defined as how many strands are cut from a 30 mm wide dough sheet (JIS). Smaller numbers give thicker noodles. Thick noodles are usually 18 or lower, thin ones 24 or 26. One machine maker lists 8 to 10 as extra-thick, 3.0 to 2.2 mm.
flavor: Spoken as 'ni-juu-ni-ban'; a lower number means thicker noodle.
use: Specified when ordering from a noodle maker. Examples: Sapporo 22, Kitakata 12 to 14, Tokyo 20 to 24.
craft: Thicker cuts are generally paired with higher hydration. Category boundaries differ among sources, so quote the number itself.
src: Aoki Shokusan: cutter number and hydration

name: Kasuiritsu (noodle hydration)
text: The ratio of water to flour. Lower hydration gives firmer, crisper noodles and higher hydration gives chewier ones. One guide groups 28 to 32 percent as low (Hakata, Jiro style), 33 to 38 percent as medium (Iekei, chuka soba) and 39 to 46 percent as high (tsukemen, Kitakata). A maker's list gives Sapporo 34 to 40, Kitakata 38 to 43 and Tokyo 33 to 36 percent.
flavor: Said as 'kasui nijuu-hachi percent'.
use: Specified with cutter number to define a noodle.
craft: The definition is not standardised: some makers count only water, others all liquid. Confirm the basis before comparing figures.
src: Aoki Shokusan: cutter number and hydration

name: Kansui
text: The alkaline agent that defines Chinese-style ramen noodles. It is dissolved in the dough water and gives the noodles their springiness, yellow colour and aroma. Home cooks sometimes substitute baking soda.
flavor: Spoken 'kansui'; refers to the alkaline salt solution in the dough.
use: Dissolved in the dough water before mixing. Wood-ash lye plays a similar role in traditional Okinawa soba.
craft: Dose affects texture, colour and aroma; give your noodle maker the target cutter number, hydration and kansui amount together. Specific percentages were not in the sources seen.
